items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (instead of), right subject is a property noun phrase, mid-sentence blank
items.passage: Instead of resting on a framework of steel trusses, ______ held rigid by their own undulating double curvature, which stiffens the thin masonry much as corrugation stiffens cardboard without adding material.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Uruguayan engineer Eladio Dieste designed warehouse roofs of reinforced brick that are
the reinforced-brick roofs of warehouses designed by Uruguayan engineer Eladio Dieste are
it is the reinforced-brick roofs of warehouses designed by Uruguayan engineer Eladio Dieste that are
Uruguayan engineer Eladio Dieste’s use of reinforced brick produced warehouse roofs that are
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something that could rest on steel trusses, which must be a roof, not a person or an activity. Choice B places “the reinforced-brick roofs” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the roofs, instead of resting on trusses, are held rigid by their own curvature.

A.why_wrong: “Uruguayan engineer Eladio Dieste” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the engineer himself might have rested on steel trusses.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, so the phrase has no noun to describe; the roofs appear only later, inside the clause.

D.recipe: nominalised subject with the agent in a possessive (N, P)
D.why_wrong: The head of the subject is “use,” so the sentence illogically says that Dieste’s use of brick might have rested on steel trusses.

items.notes: Subject: architecture and engineering (arts), Eladio Dieste’s self-supporting reinforced-brick vault roofs in Uruguay; real, known subject, no figures. Recipes W, E, N with a possessive. Section 6 checks: one-sentence passage, run 42 words with the key, 21 run words after the blank (15+); the right subject is the roofs of the buildings, one level off the obvious noun (Dieste). Each option read in the full sentence: only B gives the opener a thing that could rest on trusses. Key is not the longest option. Blind solve: B. Review check: every option read in the full sentence: only the roofs can rest on trusses; Eladio Dieste is a real, little-known subject.
band7_moves: single long run with 21 words after the blank, as in 37e5c794
right subject is a noun phrase built on the obvious noun (the roofs that Dieste designed), not the engineer the reader expects
every option names Dieste and the roofs, so the student must judge which noun phrase lands first
distractor D hides the agent in a possessive in front of a nominalised head (Dieste’s use of brick)

band7.why: Run length and the 21 words after the blank match 37e5c794, but the right subject is the plain noun the opener describes (the roofs), and each distractor fails on one visible fact (an engineer, “it,” or a “use” cannot rest on trusses). A property subject (the weight of the roofs) would let a roofs-first option stand too, since roofs can rest on trusses, so hardening it would make a second answer defensible; it stays a strong band 6, as w1b3_01.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener after a setup sentence, passive key, passage-final blank
items.passage: Rufous horneros, birds widespread in Argentina and Uruguay, construct elaborate new nests nearly every breeding season. Hardening in the sun into durable, dome-shaped enclosures of mud, straw, and dung, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: it is the nests built by these birds that swallows, finches, and other species later take over.
these birds build nests that swallows, finches, and other species later take over.
these birds’ efforts result in nests that swallows, finches, and other species later take over.
the nests built by these birds are later taken over by swallows, finches, and other species.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something that hardens in the sun into a durable enclosure of mud, straw, and dung, which must be the nests, not the birds that build them. Choice D places “the nests built by these birds” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the nests harden in the sun and are later taken over by other species.

A.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, so the phrase has no noun to describe; the nests appear only after “it is.”

B.why_wrong: “These birds” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the birds themselves dry in the sun into shells of mud, straw, and dung.

C.recipe: nominalised subject with the agent in a possessive (N, P)
C.why_wrong: The head of the subject is “efforts,” so the sentence illogically says that the birds’ efforts dry in the sun into hard shells.

items.notes: Subject (replaced in review): natural science, the rufous hornero’s oven-shaped nests of mud, straw, and dung, which other birds take over in later years; real, little-known subject, no researcher named. Setup sentence then opener and passage-final blank, as 3.5 and 3.14 (the earlier draft copied the dash-gloss skeleton of 2bca654a). Recipes E, W, N with a possessive. Each option read in the full sentence: only D gives the opener a thing that can harden into an enclosure. Options 13 to 17 words; key not the longest. Blind solve: D.
band7_moves: right subject is a noun phrase built on the obvious noun (the nests built by these birds), as in 8b017d4e and fced396a
setup sentence makes the bird the topic, so the reader expects the bird as the subject
closest distractor (B) starts with the birds and keeps every fact, so only the modifier logic separates it from the key
passive key, so the builders appear after the right subject

fixes: subject replaced: Hubert Duprat’s gold-and-pearl caddisfly cases are a widely shared (viral) art story, and the skeleton copied 2bca654a, the template’s only band-7 official (-ing opener with a dash gloss, passage-final blank, it-cleft option, key D); new subject the rufous hornero’s mud nests (claimed in claims.txt), setup sentence then opener as 3.5 and 3.14, no dash gloss; same recipes (E, W, N with a possessive) and key letter
explanation, why_wrong, subtype, notes and band7_moves rewritten; every option re-read in the full sentence: D only
safety solve: rufous horneros are not songbirds in the strict sense; 'songbird' -> 'bird'

band7.why: As 8b017d4e and fced396a: the right subject is a noun phrase built on the obvious noun (the nests built by these birds), the setup sentence makes the bird the topic, and the closest distractor (B) opens with the birds and keeps every fact, so only the modifier logic separates it from the key; options are complete, fluent clauses of 13 to 17 words.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener about how a work was composed, passage-final blank
items.passage: Indonesian novelist Pramoedya Ananta Toer spent most of the 1970s imprisoned without trial on the remote island of Buru, where for years authorities denied him writing materials. A saga initially recited aloud to fellow detainees and only later transcribed, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Pramoedya traced the political awakening of a young Javanese man under Dutch colonial rule in the Buru Quartet.
the Buru Quartet’s protagonist undergoes a political awakening as a young Javanese man under Dutch colonial rule.
the Buru Quartet traces the political awakening of a young Javanese man under Dutch colonial rule.
it is the political awakening of a young Javanese man under Dutch colonial rule that the Buru Quartet traces.
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “a saga initially recited aloud to fellow detainees and only later transcribed,” renames a work of literature. Choice C places “the Buru Quartet” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the Buru Quartet is the saga Pramoedya first recited aloud.

A.why_wrong: “Pramoedya” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the novelist himself was a saga recited aloud to detainees.

B.why_wrong: The head of the subject is “protagonist,” so the sentence illogically says that the novel’s main character was a saga recited aloud.

D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, so the phrase has no noun to describe; the Buru Quartet appears only at the end of the sentence.

items.notes: Subject: literature, Pramoedya Ananta Toer’s Buru Quartet, composed orally in the Buru prison camp (he was held there 1969 to 1979 and denied writing materials for years); real, known subject. Band 6 (no band-7 officials for R3_appositive). The appositive is about how the work was composed, not its genre, so the skeleton differs from 3.7. Recipes W, P, E. Each option read in the full sentence: only C names the saga itself after the phrase. Key is the shortest option. Blind solve: C. Review check: every option read in the full sentence: only the Buru Quartet can be “a saga”; Pramoedya and the protagonist are people, D is an it-cleft.

band7.why: R3_appositive has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7. Strong band 6 on 3.7 and 3.12: the appositive fits only the work, and the closest distractor (the Buru Quartet’s protagonist) keeps the title but makes a person the head.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head behind five singular nouns and a singular relative-clause verb, be-family options
items.passage: Commissioned by the Mughal emperor Akbar around 1562, the Hamzanama took some fifteen years to complete. The paintings that illustrate this manuscript, which recounts the legend of Amir Hamza, an uncle of the Prophet Muhammad, ______ unusually large for book illustrations of the period, each measuring roughly 70 by 55 centimeters.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the plural noun “paintings,” not “manuscript,” “legend,” or any other singular noun that comes between the subject and the blank. The plural verb “are” agrees with “paintings.”

B.why_wrong: The singular verb “is” does not agree with the plural subject “paintings”; it agrees only with the nearer singular nouns such as “uncle.”

C.why_wrong: The singular verb “was” does not agree with the plural subject “paintings.”

D.why_wrong: The singular verb “has been” does not agree with the plural subject “paintings.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (history of art), the Hamzanama, Akbar’s illustrated manuscript of about 1562 to 1577 with large paintings on cloth; real, known subject, size rounded. Section 6 checks: run 35 words (30+), 15 run words after the blank (15+), head to blank 17 words, five singular attractors (manuscript, legend, Amir Hamza, uncle, Prophet Muhammad) and a relative clause whose own verb (recounts) is singular. Every option tried in the sentence: only the plural are fits. Blind solve: A. Review check: only “are” is plural; the restrictive “that illustrate” and the plural head carry the number past five singular nouns.
band7_moves: plural head behind singular nouns, as in 3.3 (half of band-7 R1 keys are plural)
intervener with its own finite verb of the other number (which recounts), as in 0fe5ce68 and 1c65db8f
five singular attractors between head and blank, the last one right before the blank

band7.why: Matches the band-7 R1 recipe (3.3, 8a9d2f4e): plural head behind five singular nouns (manuscript, legend, Amir Hamza, uncle, Prophet Muhammad) and an intervener with its own singular verb (recounts), head 19 words from the blank; 14 run words after the blank, one short of the 15+ signal.

items.subtype: Finite main verb after a subject separated from it by a parenthetical with its own verbs
items.passage: Hungarian American chemist Mária Telkes designed the heating system for the Dover Sun House, completed in Massachusetts in 1948. Containers of Glauber’s salt (a compound that absorbs considerable heat as it melts and releases that heat as it solidifies) ______ warmth gathered by solar collectors on the building’s southern facade.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence needs a main verb for its subject, “containers of Glauber’s salt”; the verbs inside the parentheses belong to the parenthetical, not to the main clause. The finite past tense verb “stored” supplies that main verb.

A.recipe: nonfinite -ing where a finite verb is needed
A.why_wrong: The participle “storing” cannot serve as the main verb, so the sentence would be a fragment.

C.recipe: nonfinite to + base where a finite verb is needed
C.why_wrong: The infinitive “to store” cannot serve as the main verb, so the sentence would be a fragment.

D.recipe: nonfinite having + participle where a finite verb is needed
D.why_wrong: “Having stored” is a participle phrase, not a main verb, so the sentence would be a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: science and history of invention, Mária Telkes’s phase-change heat storage in the 1948 Dover Sun House; real, known subject. Band 6 (no band-7 officials for R2_finite_main). Architecture varied from 3.13: a parenthetical with four finite verbs separates the subject from the blank (19 words), not a dash list. Every option tried: only stored gives the sentence a main verb. Blind solve: B. Review check: only “stored” gives the sentence a finite main verb; the parenthetical’s verbs cannot serve.

band7.why: R2_finite_main has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7. Strong band 6 on 3.13: an 18-word parenthetical with its own verbs separates the subject from the blank.

items.subtype: Finite verb of a that-clause whose subject is separated from the blank by an interrupter with its own verb
items.passage: In the early 1990s, archaeologists surveying the site of a planned baseball stadium in Aomori, Japan, uncovered Sannai-Maruyama, an extensive Jōmon-period settlement. Their excavations revealed that hundreds of pit dwellings, along with a large structure that rested on six massive chestnut pillars, ______ part of a village inhabited for approximately 1,500 years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause beginning with “that” needs a finite verb for its subject, “hundreds of pit dwellings.” The finite verb “were” supplies it; the phrase “along with ... chestnut pillars” only interrupts the clause.

A.recipe: nonfinite -ing where a finite verb is needed
A.why_wrong: The participle “being” cannot serve as the verb of the that-clause, which would then have no finite verb.

B.recipe: nonfinite to + base where a finite verb is needed
B.why_wrong: The infinitive “to be” cannot serve as the verb of the that-clause.

C.recipe: nonfinite having + participle where a finite verb is needed
C.why_wrong: “Having been” is a participle form, so the that-clause would still lack a finite verb.

items.notes: Subject (replaced in review): history (archaeology), the Jōmon village of Sannai-Maruyama found during work for a planned stadium in Aomori; real, little-known outside Japan, no researcher named. The plan asked for band 7, but R2_finite_second has no band-7 official items, so band_target is 6. Interrupter of 12 words with its own verb (rested) between the clause subject and the blank. Every option tried: only were gives the that-clause a finite verb. Blind solve: D.

fixes: subject replaced: Caral is an encyclopedia staple (“oldest city in the Americas”) and the closing “roughly when Egypt’s Great Pyramid was erected” was a trivia coda; new subject Sannai-Maruyama (claimed in claims.txt), same interrupter shape (an along-with phrase with its own verb), options and key letter
explanation and notes rewritten; every option re-read in the full sentence: were only

band7.why: R2_finite_second has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7. Strong band 6 on 3.8 and 3daf126e: the that-clause subject sits 13 words before the blank behind an along-with phrase with its own verb (rested).

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular title head plus appositive full of plural nouns, lexical-verb options
items.passage: Atsuko Tanaka belonged to Gutai, a postwar Japanese art group known for experimental performances. Her Electric Dress (1956), a costume made from dozens of painted light bulbs and fluorescent tubes that flashed on and off, ______ later artworks that combine the human body with electronic technology.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular “Electric Dress,” which the appositive “a costume made from ...” describes. The singular verb “anticipates” agrees with it; the plural nouns “bulbs” and “tubes” belong to the appositive.

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “anticipate” does not agree with the singular subject “Electric Dress.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are anticipating” does not agree with the singular subject “Electric Dress.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have anticipated” does not agree with the singular subject “Electric Dress.”

items.notes: Subject: arts, Atsuko Tanaka’s Electric Dress (1956), a Gutai work of painted light bulbs and tubes; real, known subject. Medium: an appositive with plural nouns (dozens, bulbs, tubes) ends right before the blank. Blind solve: C. Review check: only “anticipates” is singular; Electric Dress is the head, the bulbs and tubes sit in the appositive.

items.subtype: Personal pronoun as object, singular antecedent with plural nouns nearby
items.passage: In 2016, biologists assessed the tool-using abilities of nearly every Hawaiian crow then alive, all living in captivity. Presented with a log containing morsels of food concealed in a narrow cavity, a bird would typically select a stick, insert ______ into the opening, and extract the food.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “a stick,” the thing the bird selects and inserts into the opening. The singular pronoun “it” agrees with “stick.”

B.why_wrong: The plural “them” does not agree with the singular antecedent “stick”; it could only point to “morsels of food,” which are already inside the log.

C.why_wrong: The plural “those” does not agree with the singular antecedent “stick.”

D.why_wrong: The plural “these” does not agree with the singular antecedent “stick.”

items.notes: Subject: science (animal behavior), the 2016 test of Hawaiian crow tool use, when the species survived only in captivity; real, no researcher named. Medium: plural nouns (biologists, morsels of food) sit near the pronoun, and the subject is a single bird (a bird would typically ...), so a plural pronoun has no sensible antecedent. No demonstrative this or that offered, since the stick here is a specific object. Blind solve: A. Review check: “them,” “those” and “these” could point only to the morsels, which cannot be inserted and then extracted; “it” = a stick.

items.subtype: Two-slot grid: singular possessor plus plural noun, options carry the comma before a which clause
items.passage: The Chagga people, who inhabit Mount Kilimanjaro in northern Tanzania, have long cultivated kihamba, multistory home gardens in which bananas, coffee, and vegetables flourish beneath taller shade trees. These layered gardens thrive on the ______ which receive abundant rainfall from moist winds off the Indian Ocean.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The slopes belong to one mountain, Mount Kilimanjaro, so the singular possessive “mountain’s” is needed. “Slopes” is a plain plural (the verb “receive” is plural), so it takes no apostrophe.

A.why_wrong: “Mountains” is a plain plural, not a possessive, and there is only one mountain.

B.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
B.why_wrong: “Slope’s” is possessive, but the slopes possess nothing here; the plural “slopes” is needed.

C.why_wrong: “Mountains’” is a plural possessive, but the slopes belong to a single mountain, Mount Kilimanjaro.

items.notes: Subject: social science (agriculture, anthropology), Chagga kihamba home gardens on Kilimanjaro; real, known subject. Number cues: Mount Kilimanjaro (one mountain), receive (plural slopes). Blind solve: D.

fixes: frame “occupy much of the ______” echoed official 1.16 (“many of the ______”), the echo the b3 review fixed; now “thrive on the ______”; options and key unchanged
every option re-read in the full sentence: mountain’s lower slopes, only

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head plus participial phrase and appositive with plural nouns, be-family options
items.passage: Japanese merchant Inō Tadataka began studying astronomy and surveying after retiring, and from 1800 to 1816 he and his assistants measured the country’s coastlines. The resulting map, a set of more than 200 sheets completed in 1821, ______ so accurate that it remained in use for decades.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “map”; “a set of more than 200 sheets completed in 1821” describes it. The singular verb “was” agrees with “map.”

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” does not agree with the singular subject “map”; it agrees only with the nearer plural “sheets.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” does not agree with the singular subject “map.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” does not agree with the singular subject “map.”

items.notes: Subject: history (history of science), Inō Tadataka’s survey of Japan’s coastline (1800 to 1816) and the map completed in 1821; real, known subject, sheet count rounded to more than 200. Medium: plural attractor (200 sheets) between head and blank, after plural assistants and coastlines in the previous clause. Blind solve: B. Review check: only “was” is singular; “a set of more than 200 sheets” is an appositive to “map”.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener, passive key, mid-sentence blank
items.passage: Mathematician Paulus Gerdes spent decades studying sona, geometric figures that storytellers of the Chokwe people in northeastern Angola have traditionally traced in sand. Drawn as a single continuous line that loops around a grid of dots, ______ to illustrate proverbs, fables, and riddles.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: these figures are often sketched by a storyteller
a storyteller will often sketch these figures
it is a storyteller who often sketches these figures
Gerdes found that storytellers often sketch these figures
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something drawn as a single continuous line, which must be the figures, not a person. Choice A places “these figures” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the figures are drawn as one continuous line.

B.why_wrong: “A storyteller” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the storyteller is drawn as a continuous line.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, so the phrase has no noun to describe.

D.why_wrong: “Gerdes” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the mathematician was drawn as a continuous line around a grid of dots.

items.notes: Subject: social science (ethnomathematics), Chokwe sona sand drawings studied by Paulus Gerdes; real, known subject. Passive key, as 2.2 and 3.12 use; recipes W, E, W. Key is not the longest option. Blind solve: A. Review check: only the figures can be drawn as a line; B and D make a person the subject, C is an it-cleft.

items.subtype: Nonfinite -ing phrase of result after a complete clause and comma
items.passage: In the 1090s, Chinese statesman Su Song oversaw the construction of an astronomical clock tower in Kaifeng, the Song dynasty’s capital. Inside the tower, a waterwheel rotated in small, regular increments, ______ a bronze armillary sphere on the rooftop and mechanical figures that rang bells and struck drums to announce the hours.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “a waterwheel rotated in small, regular increments” is already complete, so the words after the comma must form a phrase that modifies it, not a second verb with no conjunction. The participle “driving” begins that phrase.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
A.why_wrong: The finite verb “drove” after a comma, with no conjunction, creates an ungrammatical string of two verbs for one subject.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
B.why_wrong: The finite verb “had driven” after a comma, with no conjunction, creates the same error.

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
D.why_wrong: The finite present verb “drives” also lacks a conjunction and shifts from the past tense of the passage.

items.notes: Subject: history (history of technology), Su Song’s water-driven clock tower in Kaifeng; real, known subject. The object follows the blank directly, so drove cannot be read as a passive participle. Blind solve: C. Review check: “drove,” “had driven” and “drives” after the comma make a run-on (two finite verbs, no conjunction), as 2.9’s “earned”; only “driving” fits.

items.subtype: Personal pronoun as object of a preposition, plural antecedent
items.passage: In dry parts of southeastern Kenya, communities build sand dams, low concrete walls across seasonal riverbeds. When rains come, floodwater carries sand that piles up behind ______, and water stored in the sand remains available for months after the river runs dry.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “sand dams,” the walls that sand piles up behind. The plural pronoun “them” agrees with this plural antecedent.

A.why_wrong: The singular “it” does not agree with the plural antecedent “sand dams”; the only nearby singular noun, “floodwater,” makes no sense here, since sand does not pile up behind floodwater.

C.why_wrong: The singular “this” does not agree with the plural antecedent “sand dams.”

D.why_wrong: The singular “that” does not agree with the plural antecedent “sand dams.”

items.notes: Subject: science and engineering (water supply), sand dams in southeastern Kenya; real, general description. Easy: the only plausible antecedent is the plural sand dams (walls); no singular noun before the blank can sensibly have sand pile up behind it. Blind solve: B.

fixes: why_wrong A now names the one singular noun “it” could point to (floodwater) and why it fails
every option re-read in the full sentence: them only

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head with a reduced relative ending in a singular noun before the blank, be-family options
items.passage: Raffia textiles made by the Kuba people of central Africa ______ recognized for their bold geometric patterns, which women embroider onto plain cloth woven by men.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the plural noun “textiles” (the words “made by ... central Africa” only describe them, and “their” later in the sentence refers back to them). The plural verb “are” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: The singular verb “is” does not agree with the plural subject “textiles”; it agrees only with the nearby “central Africa.”

B.why_wrong: The singular verb “was” does not agree with the plural subject “textiles.”

C.why_wrong: The singular verb “has been” does not agree with the plural subject “textiles.”

items.notes: Subject (replaced in review): arts (textiles), Kuba raffia cloth, woven by men and embroidered by women; real, little-known subject, no names or figures. Easy: plural head, one singular noun next to the blank, as 1.7. Blind solve: D.

fixes: subject replaced: the 1,300-year-old sacred lotus seed is record trivia, and a named researcher with a year on an easy agreement item was a round-2 tell; new subject Kuba raffia textiles (claimed in claims.txt); plural head, options is / was / has been / are, key letter unchanged
explanation, why_wrong, subtype and notes rewritten; every option re-read in the full sentence: are only

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular proper-noun subject right before the blank, be-family options
items.passage: Sungbo’s Eredo ______ a vast ring of ditches and earthen embankments that extends for roughly 160 kilometers around the town of Ijebu-Ode in southwestern Nigeria.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is “Sungbo’s Eredo,” the name of a single structure, which the sentence calls “a vast ring” (and “extends” agrees with it). The singular verb “is” agrees with it.

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” does not agree with the singular subject “Sungbo’s Eredo.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” does not agree with the singular subject “Sungbo’s Eredo.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” does not agree with the singular subject “Sungbo’s Eredo.”

items.notes: Subject: history (archaeology), Sungbo’s Eredo, the rampart and ditch system around Ijebu-Ode, Nigeria; real, little-known subject. Review changed the predicate from “one of the largest earthworks in Africa”, the frame of 1.40 (“one of the rare places in the world”). Easy: no intervener; the singular predicate “a vast ring ... that extends” confirms the number. Blind solve: A.

fixes: predicate “______ one of the largest earthworks in Africa” copied the frame of 1.40 (“______ one of the rare places in the world”); now “______ a vast ring of ditches and earthen embankments that extends ...”; options and key unchanged
explanation and notes updated; every option re-read in the full sentence: is only

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular subject (region of X) right before the blank, lexical-verb options
items.passage: Rosalía de Castro’s Cantares gallegos (1863) helped revive literature in Galician, a language closely related to Portuguese. Every year on May 17, the anniversary of the collection’s publication, the Spanish region of Galicia ______ Galician Literature Day.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “region.” The singular verb “celebrates” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “celebrate” does not agree with the singular subject “region.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are celebrating” does not agree with the singular subject “region.”
